issues.description: In Experiment 1, 40 participants remained after training exclusions. The analysis section states that exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials 'resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded).' However, 23 + 5 = 28, not 40. Either 17 participants were excluded (40 - 23 = 17), or 35 were included (40 - 5 = 35). The reported numbers are internally inconsistent, and 12 participants are unaccounted for.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (5 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.description: The Experiment 1 Procedure section states participants indicated confidence on a 2-point scale ('from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain'), but the Figure 1 caption describes a 4-point scale ('1 = guess, 4 = certainty'). This directly contradicts the procedure description and creates ambiguity about how 'high confidence' trials were defined and filtered. Experiment 2 explicitly uses a 1-4 scale, making cross-experiment comparisons problematic if Experiment 1 truly used a different scale.
issues.quote: participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of two boxes (from 1-2, 1 = guess, 2 = certain)

issues.description: Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory errors in Experiment 2) reports BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay, which constitutes strong evidence AGAINST including Memory Delay. However, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay),' indicating strong evidence FOR Memory Delay. These values are off by a factor of ~3000 and point in opposite directions. Additionally, Table 4 shows Target Type with BFincl = 39110.895, but the text claims 'only Memory Delay was a relevant factor,' ignoring this massive Target Type effect. The table and text appear to describe entirely different analyses.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42, see Appendix 1 for a full model comparison and Table 4 for an overview of BFincl for each model component). Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)

issues.description: The Experiment 4 results section states 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials,' but Figure 5 is already used for Experiment 3. The actual figure for Experiment 4 is captioned 'Figure 6 Experiment 4.' This mismatch could confuse readers and suggests incomplete manuscript proofing.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.description: Exclusion rates based on the high-confidence trial criterion are extremely high: Experiment 1 excludes up to 42.5% of participants (17 of 40, or at minimum the reported 5), Experiment 2 excludes 31.7% (92 of 290). These rates raise serious concerns about selection bias—the included sample may not be representative, as it systematically retains participants who were more confident (and possibly more task-engaged or more susceptible to the experimental manipulation). The excluded participants had markedly different confidence rates (e.g., 15.7% vs 49.2% in Experiment 2), suggesting systematic differences between included and excluded groups.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The primary analyses are restricted to high-confidence trials only, which is a post-treatment variable (determined after the experimental manipulation). Conditioning on confidence can introduce collider bias: for example, if both accurate memory and expectation-driven guessing can produce high confidence, then restricting to high-confidence trials artificially enriches the sample with expectation-driven responses in conditions where memory is weaker (longer delays). This could create or inflate the observed pattern of increasing 'illusory' errors over time without requiring any actual memory illusion mechanism. The authors should analyze all trials and model confidence as a dependent variable or mediator, rather than using it as a filter.
issues.quote: we exclude the possibility that the errors are a result of guessing in the absence of reliable memories / reliable perception by focusing on high confidence errors: errors where the participant explicitly indicates to know the answer

issues.subcategory: Temporal increase conflated with memory illusion
issues.description: The central causal argument is that increasing errors over time proves these are 'memory illusions' rather than perceptual errors, because perceptual errors should remain constant. However, this logic has an important flaw: partially or imprecisely encoded percepts (degraded perceptual representations) could also become less distinguishable over time as the trace decays. A weakly encoded percept of a pseudo-letter might be reported correctly when probed immediately (when some bottom-up signal remains) but reported as the real letter later (when the weak trace has further decayed). This is not a 'memory illusion' in the sense of an active reshaping by expectations—it is simply differential decay of weak vs. strong memory traces. The temporal increase alone cannot distinguish active top-down reshaping from passive differential decay.
issues.quote: If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed.

issues.subcategory: Asymmetry explanation conflates encoding strength with world knowledge
issues.description: The asymmetry between pseudo-to-real errors and real-to-pseudo errors is attributed to 'world knowledge,' but an equally parsimonious explanation is differential encoding quality. Real letters have stronger, more robust memory representations simply because they are more familiar stimuli—they are encoded more precisely and deeply. Pseudo-letters, being unfamiliar, are encoded more weakly and are therefore more prone to any type of degradation or confusion. The 'world knowledge' interpretation implies active top-down reshaping, while differential encoding implies passive advantages for familiar stimuli. The experiments do not distinguish between these mechanisms.
issues.quote: high confidence errors occurred mainly for pseudo-to-real letter memories, and much less often for real-to-pseudo-letter memories, indicating that visual similarity is not the primary cause of this memory-bias. Instead 'world knowledge' (e.g., which orientation letters usually have) appear to drive these STM illusions.

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the dismissal of response bias is circular: 'this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.' No formal analysis (e.g., signal detection theory to separate sensitivity from bias, or analysis of response proportions on catch trials) is offered to rule out response bias. Since real letters are more familiar and might simply be preferred responses, this is a critical alternative explanation. In Experiments 1-2, real letters were more prevalent in the stimulus set, potentially further encouraging a bias to select real letters.
issues.quote: However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias.

issues.subcategory: Flawed dismissal of Fuzzy Trace Theory
issues.description: The authors argue that FTT is inconsistent with their data because 'high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories... The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.' This logic is backwards: FTT predicts that high similarity INCREASES false memories, so abundant false memories with high-similarity stimuli would SUPPORT FTT, not contradict it. The actual argument the authors seem to intend—that the ASYMMETRY between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors cannot be explained by similarity alone (since similarity is symmetric)—is never clearly articulated. As stated, the FTT dismissal is logically incoherent.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online, meaning stimulus display conditions (screen size, resolution, viewing distance, refresh rate, ambient lighting, hardware-specific timing accuracy) were uncontrolled. Stimulus sizes specified in degrees of visual angle are meaningless without controlled viewing distance. Timing precision for brief displays (250 ms) on consumer hardware through a web browser is known to be unreliable. These factors could differentially affect perception and encoding of pseudo-letters vs. real letters, yet no limitations or validation checks (e.g., timing accuracy verification) are reported.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration and variable stopping rules
issues.description: None of the four experiments mention pre-registration. Experiments 3 and 4 use Bayesian sequential stopping rules, but with different thresholds (BF > 6 for Experiment 3, BF > 10 for Experiment 4) applied to a specific t-test comparison, without justification for the different thresholds or for selecting that particular test as the criterion. The choice of which comparison to use for the stopping rule, the threshold values, and the analysis plan (including the specific ANOVA models, exclusion criteria, and follow-up tests) appear to have been determined by the researchers without pre-specification, introducing substantial researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop... once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop

issues.description: The exclusion criterion of '10 trials or less' per cell for high-confidence trials appears arbitrary and is not justified or derived from a power analysis. Different thresholds would include different numbers of participants and potentially yield different results. No sensitivity analysis is presented showing robustness across different exclusion thresholds. Given the massive impact of this criterion (e.g., 92 of 290 participants excluded in Experiment 2), this represents a major undisclosed researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis

issues.description: No standardized effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, eta-squared, or credible intervals for parameter estimates) are reported for any analysis across the four experiments. Only Bayes Factors and raw percentages are provided. Effect sizes are essential for evaluating practical significance, comparing across experiments, and enabling future meta-analyses or power analyses.
issues.quote: The Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA showed that a model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, and Memory Delay, and a Target Type * Error Type and Memory Delay * Error Type interaction had the best fit (BFm = 18)

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the 'Short with interference' condition presents the cue simultaneously with the irrelevant second display, while in the 'Short' and 'Long' conditions the cue appears alone. This means the interference condition differs from the Short condition not only in visual interference but also in dual-task demands (parsing the cue from the interfering display) and attentional load. These confounds make it impossible to attribute differences solely to memory interference.
issues.quote: If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition).

issues.subcategory: High confidence does not guarantee memory illusion
issues.description: The authors equate 'high confidence errors' with 'illusory memories,' assuming that high confidence necessarily indicates the participant has an actual (false) memory trace. However, high confidence can arise from other sources: strong prior expectations (the participant reasons 'it's probably a real letter' and is confident in that reasoning), familiarity-based responding (the real letter 'feels right' without an actual memorial experience), or metacognitive miscalibration. Without phenomenological measures (e.g., remember/know judgments), the construct of 'illusory memory' as distinct from confident inference cannot be validated.
issues.quote: Illusory memories should result in high confidence erroneous responses, where the participants has access to a memory trace (albeit an incorrect memory trace).

issues.description: All four experiments use only letters/pseudo-letters as stimuli. The General Discussion claims these findings have broad implications for vision research, STM, and predictive processing in general, and suggests 'memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general.' However, letters are a special stimulus category with unique properties (overlearned, categorical, verbally encodable) that may not generalize to other visual stimuli. The authors acknowledge this only tentatively and through reference to other work, not through their own experimental evidence.
issues.quote: it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general. This implicates that very early illusory memories could be an inherent feature of the cognitive processing sequence for sensory input.

issues.subcategory: Missing information on trial counts per cell
issues.description: The number of critical trials per participant per cell after all exclusions and the high-confidence filter is not reported. Given the complex designs (e.g., Experiment 1: 3 delays × 2 target types × 2 error types, from ~220 critical trials total before high-confidence filtering), the number of observations per cell could be very small, raising concerns about the reliability of the percentage estimates. The total number of critical trials (~220) divided across cells could yield as few as ~18 trials per cell before confidence filtering.
issues.quote: Together, the critical trials made up ~220 trials, 26% of all trials in the experiment.

issues.description: Experiments 2-4 recruited first-year psychology students for course credit, and sample sizes were determined by course enrollment (Experiment 2) or stopping rules. Experiment 2's sample had a very wide age range (18-56) suggesting non-standard student demographics. The results may not generalize beyond this WEIRD, psychology-student population. Additionally, familiarity with the Latin alphabet is assumed but not verified, which could matter for non-native speakers in a Dutch university.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum. The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course

issues.subcategory: No assessment of awareness of experimental manipulation
issues.description: Only Experiment 2 includes a post-experiment questionnaire about awareness of the experimental purpose, and only regarding the cue-color manipulation. No experiment assesses whether participants became aware of the pseudo-letter manipulation itself (e.g., realized that the experiment was specifically testing confusion between real and pseudo-letters). Such awareness could lead to strategic responding that differs from naive performance. The explicit instruction 'not to confuse real and pseudo-letters' may have paradoxically increased attention to this distinction in ways that either inflate or deflate the effect.
issues.quote: They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of non-illusory errors across Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2's main results, the text states that 'the other (non-illusory) error rate was not influenced by target-type (11% for real-letter and pseudo-letter targets).' However, the Table 4 follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory errors shows an enormous BFincl for Target Type (39110.895), which would indicate a very strong effect of Target Type on non-illusory errors—directly contradicting the text's claim of no influence. If the table is correct, the interpretation throughout the paper that asymmetric errors are specific to illusory (not other) errors would be undermined.
issues.quote: the other (non-illusory) error rate was not influenced by target-type (11% for real-letter and pseudo-letter targets)

issues.subcategory: Confound between time delay and memory decay
issues.description: The authors interpret the increase in illusory errors from short to long delays as evidence that 'world knowledge' actively reshapes memory. However, delay and decay are confounded: longer delays produce weaker memory traces. If participants with degraded memory traces simply default to selecting the more familiar option (a real letter) as a guessing strategy—even while reporting high confidence—this would produce the same pattern without any active reshaping of memory content. The design cannot separate active memory transformation from confidence-calibrated guessing with familiar defaults.
issues.quote: as the quality of the memory representation decreases through decay or interference, world knowledge plays an increasingly large role within STM

issues.description: Overall accuracy rates (proportion correct) for each experiment and condition are not reported. Without knowing the base rate of correct responses, it is difficult to contextualize the error rates. For instance, knowing whether accuracy was 60% or 90% fundamentally changes interpretation of a 20% illusory error rate. The percentage of high-confidence trials is reported, but not the overall task performance.
issues.quote: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in 70% of high confidence trials

issues.description: Follow-up analyses vary across experiments without clear justification. In Experiment 2, separate ANOVAs are conducted for illusory and non-illusory errors to decompose the three-way interaction. In Experiment 1, the three-way interaction has only 'anecdotal evidence' (BFincl = 2.45) but is nonetheless discussed at length. The selective decomposition and emphasis on different aspects of the results across experiments could reflect post-hoc analytic choices.
issues.quote: Finally, there is only anecdotal evidence for a three-way interaction between Target Type, Error Type and Memory Delay (BFincl = 2.45): For pseudo-letter targets, illusory errors increase 12% as memory deteriorates

issues.subcategory: Missing details on letter selection and counterbalancing
issues.description: The specific letters used in the experiments are not listed. Since only asymmetric letters were included (excluding A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y), the remaining set is B, C, D, E, F, G, J, K, L, N, P, Q, R, S, Z. However, some of these (e.g., S, Z) have mirror images that may still look like plausible letters or be less obviously 'pseudo.' No analysis of item-level effects is provided, and there is no discussion of whether particular letter identities drove the results.
issues.quote: the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays
